newsitem.title: USA: AT&T in merger talks with SBC - source.
newsitem.headline: AT&T in merger talks with SBC - source.

text.p: AT&T Corp. is in merger talks with SBC Communications Inc. on a deal that would remake the communications landscape by propelling AT&T back into the local phone business, a source familiar with the talks said Tuesday.

The talks, which involve top officials at both companies, have been held from time to time for at least a year, but the pace has accelerated in the past month with key executives speaking almost daily, the source said.
However, many issues remain to be hammered out, including the combined company's executive structure. No deal is immiment for several weeks at least, the source said.
AT&T, the nation's largest long-distance carrier, and SBC, currently the nation's largest provider of local phone services, declined to comment on whether talks were under way.

News of the possible merger caused AT&T stocks to surge $1.375 Tuesday to $37.50 in active trading on the New York Stock Exchange and buoyed Baby Bells amid speculation a deal could spur a new round of mega-mergers. SBC rose 75 cents to $57.625, also on the NYSE.
A report Tuesday in The Wall Street Journal said a merger of the two companies would be worth more than $50 billion, based on SBC's stock valuation at the close of trading Friday.

The CNBC financial cable TV channel reported Tuesday a plan was under discussion in which AT&T President John Walter would become chief executive of the combined companies and SBC Chairman and Chief Executive Ed Whitacre would be non-executive chairman, with a strategic planning role.

Walters, a longtime publishing industry executive, has been with AT&T for seven months. Whitacre, the widely respected chief executive of SBC since 1990, has worked for SBC and its Southwestern Bell predecessor for 32 years.

Many Wall Street and industry analysts said any deal still could get hung up over financial or management structure details or the severe antitrust scrutiny a merger would likely face from federal and state regulators.

The acquisition of SBC would give AT&T a commanding presence in local markets, including California and Texas, and would extend AT&T's wireless subscriber base in seven of the top 10 major U.S. metropolitan markets.
AT&T Wireless was the nation's largest provider of cellular phone services at the end of 1996, while SBC was neck and neck with Bell Atlantic NYNEX Mobile in a race for second.

Merrill Lynch telecommunications analyst Dan Reingold said in a published commentary that while it is "entirely possible" the two have held talks, "we ascribe a low probability of ultimate approval because of the implications for competition."

Southwestern Bell Telephone was an operating unit of AT&T until the old Bell system monopoly was broken up in 1984 under a federal antitrust decree that created the Baby Bells and prohibited AT&T from entering the local service business.
Passage of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 ended the prohibition against AT&T's participation in the local phone business.

However, analysts said that under the new legislation, the merger of AT&T and SBC is unlikely to receive regulatory approval until SBC can demonstrate it has opened its local phone markets to substantial competition.
"This deal would be great news for AT&T," said Daniel Briere, president of TeleChoice, an industry consulting group in Verona, N.J. "It's just not necessarily great news for the marketplace."
Briere said a variety of factors could derail what would be a massive deal in the several years it will likely take to win regulatory approval and complete the integration of the organisations.

These hurdles would hamper the two at a time when far-reaching changes are sweeping through the industry, reducing their competitiveness in new markets even as business restrictions are lifted from other challengers, he said.
A deal would be complicated by SBC's $16.7 billion acquisition in April of Pacific Telesis Group, another regional Bell company. The merger of the two Baby Bells has only begun to get under way.

The regulatory issues alone raised by any effort by AT&T to reassemble even part of the old Bell monopoly system may be enough to scuttle the deal, several analysts said. AT&T would receive special scrutiny because of this history, they agreed.

"It's not a question of if they are going to be handcuffed, but whether they will be shackled or put in solitary confinement," Briere said of the restraints regulators were likely to put on the merger to allay competitive concerns.
The merger talks between AT&T and SBC drew harsh criticism from corporate rivals, consumer advocacy groups and Reed Hundt, outgoing chairman of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission.
Hundt told a news conference Tuesday the reported deal's scale raised questions. "Obviously, it calls the following question into mind, which is, 'Where's the line?'"

LCI International Inc., a leading supplier of long distance phone and data services, said in a statement that such a deal would violate the spirit of recently passed U.S. laws that are designed to promote competiton in local markets.
"Over a year after the Telecom Act has passed, competition in local phone markets is not even close to being a reality," LCI Chairman Brian Thompson said.
"Until that monopoly is broken ... mergers between long-distance and local giants ... must not be allowed to go forward," he said.
